newsitem.title: DUBAI: No bikinis, but Saudi promotes tourism anyway.
newsitem.headline: No bikinis, but Saudi promotes tourism anyway.

text.p: Don't expect bikini-clad women on beaches, gambling in casinos or drinking the night away at bars.
But Saudi Arabia, the Moslem Gulf state better known for its black gold -- oil -- wants tourists to visit its deserts, beaches and mountains in what it calls "domestic tourism".

"Tourism is a money-generating industry, which we should utilise. We are just at the beginning of the road," said Khalid Rabah al-Harbi, director of the department of tourism at the Jeddah Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

"We are concentrating on domestic tourism and tourism from Gulf countries due to the special situation of visas in the kingdom. There is no trend to encourage foreign tourists," said Harbi, who is also a member of the National Tourism Committee.
Gulf Arabs do not need visas to visit Saudi Arabia. Other foreigners can only get visas through a Saudi sponsor and rarely can they do that through Saudi embassies.

Industry experts say Westerners would not be targeted in the new tourism campaign in a country where women have to cover up and are not allowed to drive and alchohol, gambling and mixing of single men and women are banned under Islamic norms.
"There is no way that they would open the doors to your average Western tourist," one expert said.
SAUDIS SPEND MORE THAN OTHER TOURISTS

Abdul-Mohsen al-Hakir, chairman of the private National Tourism Committee, said in recent remarks in the Saudi press that Saudi tourists spend 10 times more abroad than American tourists and 12 times more than European travellers.
The latest official statistics show that in 1995 two million Saudis went on holiday abroad spending $8 billion, Harbi said.
"If we can attract 10 to 20 percent of this towards domestic tourism it will be an achievement," he said.

Armed with petrodollars, Saudis are used to vacationing abroad, mostly in Europe and Asia, on average three times a year. Summer is especially popular, as people try to escape searing temperatures at home.
That, however, is changing with government spending cuts due to weak oil prices until early 1996 denting consumer confidence.

More Saudis are looking for local vacations and need places to do that. The small tourism industry is also seeking to cater to the needs of a fast growing, mostly youthful population, in a country of 18 million, including six million expatriates.
Harbi said more Saudis are looking into holidaying at home due to "growing awareness" and not financial reasons.

"It is not a question of less money, there is more awareness now that Saudis can spend holidays here," he said. "Travel agents are being encouraged to organise domestic tourism packages which they did not do before."
Experts question how successful the campaign will be in attracting Saudis, some of whom admit they travel abroad to enjoy some of the social freedoms lacking in their own country.
"Many Saudis like to vacation abroad, where they can let their hair down a bit," one said.
FANCY VISITING PETROCHEMICAL COMPLEXES?
New tourist developments worth about 15 million riyals ($4 million) are being built, including two huge Red Sea projects comprising entertainment cities and villa complexes, they say.

Officials speak of the infant industry opening up scope for investments. They cite modern communications, roads, clean beaches, historic sites like Mecca and Medina -- two of Islam's holiest shrines -- and the mountains of Asir, Abha and Taif.
But an added attraction is being advertised.
The Saudi Gazette daily in September 1996 reported the Holiday Inn hotel in the eastern city of Jubail was promoting the Jubail industrial city as a tourist attraction.

"You can see world-class petrochemical complexes, the pride of Saudi Arabia, the huge oil refineries, industrial companies," the hotel said. It added men and women would be taken on tours on separate buses and tourists "will have to abide by a number of restrictions, including the prohibition of taking of photos in the industrial zone".
"RELIGIOUS TOURISM" INTEGRAL TO INDUSTRY
The officials also speak of "religious tourism".
Harbi said 5.5 million visas were granted in 1996 to Moslems outside the kingdom to perform the annual haj pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina and umrah, a minor pilgrimage.

"If we can attract 15 or 20 percent of them who have time and money to spend time in Jeddah (in the Western region) it will be good," he said. "Their visas do not allow them out of the Western region so they cannot tour other areas in the kingdom."
"Also we are trying to attract expatriates who live in the kingdom to tour sites during the weekends," he added.
The officials also speak of the industry opening up doors for private sector investments and more jobs for Saudi nationals -- two of the government's economic goals.
Harbi said the government was currently considering setting up an official tourism body to coordinate the efforts of the existing private sector bodies.
